units.text: `emulateSavedInstanceStateRestore()` saves all the state stored via savedInstanceState or `rememberSaveable`, disposes current composition, and composes again the content passed to `StateRestorationTester.setContent`. units.text: Android's Robolectric page says you can simulate the launch of an Activity and test the logic inside it, calling all the lifecycle methods. In its UI testing section, right after the sentence "Any UI test present in the `test` source set runs with Robolectric.", it shows an Espresso example that destroys and recreates the Activity with `scenario.recreate()`:

quotes.quote: you can simulate the launch of an Activity and test the logic inside it, calling all the lifecycle methods.
Any UI test present in the test source set runs with Robolectric.
// Destroy and recreate Activity scenario.recreate()

units.text: A Robolectric blog post, which describes itself as "an outside read of the code as it stands in mid-2026, not an official AndroidX position", says a ViewModel needs a ViewModelStoreOwner + SavedStateRegistryOwner + lifecycle from its host, and the hardest thing to test is process death. `viewModelScenario { }` fabricates that owner trio in-memory and exposes `recreate()`:

quotes.quote: This is an outside read of the code as it stands in mid-2026, not an official AndroidX position

A ViewModel needs a ViewModelStoreOwner + SavedStateRegistryOwner + lifecycle from its host, and the hardest thing to test is process death. viewModelScenario { } fabricates that owner trio in-memory and exposes recreate()

units.text:
viewModelScenario { TestViewModel(handle = createSavedStateHandle()) }.use { scenario ->
    scenario.viewModel.handle["key"] = "value"
    scenario.recreate()                                  // simulate process death
    assertThat(scenario.viewModel.handle.get<String>("key")).isEqualTo("value")
}

units.text: The same blog post says `recreate()` round-trips the saved state through a real Parcel (and enforces the 1 MB Binder limit), reproducing real serialization loss rather than an in-memory copy.
